analysis.one_liner: Offers grants to states that require police bias training and independent prosecutors for police deadly-force cases.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors, having received only a referral and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a new federal grant program run by the Attorney General. A state could get the money each year only if it requires annual bias and sensitivity training for police officers (covering racial bias, cultural diversity, and dealing with disabled, mentally ill, and immigrant residents) and passes a law requiring an outside prosecutor — one who does not live or work in the county where the incident happened — to handle criminal cases where an officer's use of deadly force kills or injures someone. States that skip either requirement simply become ineligible for the grant.
analysis.who_benefits: People in states that adopt the requirements: officers would get recurring training on racial bias, cultural diversity, and interacting with disabled, mentally ill, and immigrant residents, and deadly-force cases involving police would be investigated and prosecuted by an outside prosecutor rather than the local one, who works alongside the police department involved. The families of people killed or injured by police in participating states would see those cases handled by a prosecutor with no ties to the local department. States would also receive federal grant money for doing so.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states adopting police accountability rules

how_it_helps.text: Requires all law enforcement officers in participating states to complete an annual sensitivity training session covering ethnic and racial bias, cultural diversity, and police interaction with the disabled, mentally ill, and new immigrants — 8 hours for academy recruits and 4 hours for current officers, with states certifying completion to the Attorney General [S2].

Conditions grant money on a state enacting an 'independent prosecution of law enforcement law,' under which an outside prosecutor — someone who neither lives nor works in the county where the incident occurred and would not normally handle the case — must conduct any criminal investigation and prosecution of an officer's use of deadly force that caused death or injury [S2].

The independent-prosecutor mechanism addresses a well-known structural problem: local prosecutors depend on police departments to build their cases, so they rarely bring charges against officers, and this bill would move those cases to a prosecutor with no ties to the local department [S2].

The Attorney General could make a grant to each participating state every fiscal year to carry out the training and independent-prosecution requirements, giving states money rather than merely imposing mandates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grants. Participating states would bear the cost of providing annual training to every academy recruit and active officer and of administering a system for appointing outside prosecutors in deadly-force cases; states that decline give up only the grant money. Police departments would face the recurring training requirement, and in adopting states, local prosecutors would lose jurisdiction over cases involving officers' use of deadly force.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, state police budgets, local prosecutors

drawbacks.text: The bill is purely an incentive: a state that does not want the requirements loses nothing except eligibility for the grant, so there is no way to make any state participate, and even a participating state's obligation is tied to a one-year grant term that could lapse [S2].

The training requirement is modest — 4 hours a year for serving officers and 8 hours for recruits — and critics of sensitivity training would argue that a few classroom hours do little to change officer conduct [S2].

States get a compliance window of just 120 days after enactment (with a possible 120-day extension for good-faith efforts), a tight timeline for overhauling training programs and writing independent-prosecution statutes [S2].

Removing deadly-force cases from local prosecutors to an outside prosecutor in another county adds cost and complexity and, in the view of defenders of local prosecutors, second-guesses officers' split-second decisions through the criminal justice system [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits are real but limited: the bill addresses two of the most persistent complaints about American policing — inadequate bias training and the conflict of interest when a local prosecutor decides whether to charge a local officer — and it does so by paying states rather than forcing them. But the design undercuts the ambition. Because compliance is voluntary and the only penalty is losing a small, one-year grant, most states could simply opt out, and the bill does nothing at all in states that decline. It would likely move only states already inclined to act. As drafted, it is a modest nudge, not a reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2024, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and sat there with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, late in the 118th Congress, with roughly five months left before the session expired in January 2025 [S1].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; that was the only action ever taken on it [S4].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor count stayed at zero [S3].
The Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor, so it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1, S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one who wanted police accountability changes gained anything; the status quo held. Law enforcement organizations and local prosecutors who prefer the existing arrangement — where local prosecutors decide whether to charge local officers and training standards are set by states — are better off because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; police unions and local prosecutors

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, his proposal to pay states for police sensitivity training and independent prosecution of deadly-force cases

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it unconsidered for the rest of the Congress

against.name: House colleagues of Rep. Cohen
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with no demonstrated support

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only partisan signal is that a lone Democrat sponsored it and no Republican (and no other Democrat) cosponsored it.

industries.note: If states took the deal, police officers would face mandatory annual sensitivity training and deadly-force cases would go to outside prosecutors instead of the local ones who work with their departments. Because participation was voluntary, unions could avoid these changes simply by lobbying states to decline the grants.

In participating states, prosecutors would lose authority over the most sensitive cases they handle — whether to charge an officer for a deadly-force death or injury — with those cases assigned to an outside prosecutor. Some local prosecutors favor such independence; the dominant incentive, though, is to keep charging discretion over the departments they rely on.
